title: The Unregulated Crisis: Why Vietnam's Dog Meat Trade Poses a Public Health Emergency
excerpt: Zero registered slaughterhouses. No food safety oversight. Vietnam's unregulated dog meat supply chain creates ideal conditions for rabies, E. coli, and Salmonella transmission—a public health crisis hiding in plain sight.
body_html:
Vietnam has a food safety problem most regulators refuse to acknowledge: zero registered dog meat slaughterhouses. This isn't an oversight—it's a regulatory vacuum that endangers millions of Vietnamese citizens every single year.

Unlike chicken, pork, or seafood, which flow through inspected facilities with documented safety protocols, dog meat moves through completely unregulated supply chains. Animals are slaughtered in backyard facilities, transported in unsanitary conditions, and sold in unmonitored markets. The result: ideal conditions for disease transmission. Rabies exposure from unvaccinated animals. E. coli contamination from poor hygiene. Salmonella cross-contamination in shared food preparation spaces. These aren't theoretical risks—they're documented public health threats that other nations have already eliminated.

When South Korea banned dog meat consumption in 2019, public health officials noted an immediate reduction in foodborne illness clusters previously traced to the trade. Switzerland's comprehensive ban in 1981 included rigorous enforcement that removed this disease vector entirely. Taiwan's ban, enacted in 2017, specifically cited rabies transmission risk as a regulatory priority. These countries didn't ban dog meat because sentiment shifted—they banned it because data demanded action.

The encouraging news: 95% of Vietnamese citizens already support ending this trade (2021 survey). This isn't Western pressure. This is Vietnamese families, Vietnamese food safety experts, and Vietnamese public health officials recognizing that regulation without registered facilities is an impossible task. Formalizing a ban transforms an unregulated crisis into a closed chapter, aligning policy with both public will and scientific evidence.

Real food safety requires real enforcement. Vietnam deserves both.
